tbl3_1: A five-row table listing x, the exact solution, the three-coefficient collocation approximation, and their error at x equal to minus one, minus one half, zero, one half, and one; the error is zero at the endpoints and reaches about minus two times ten to the power minus two near the interior, showing the low-order approximation is accurate to a couple percent.
fig3_1: Two side-by-side line plots over the interval from minus one to one. Left panel: the exact solution u of x equals e to the power x squared minus one plotted against the three-coefficient collocation approximation; the two curves are nearly indistinguishable U-shapes rising from about 0.37 at the center to one at the endpoints, with the three collocation points at minus one half, zero, and one half marked by squares. Right panel: the difference exact minus approximate, a smooth oscillatory error curve that crosses zero exactly at the three collocation points and the endpoints, peaking around two times ten to the power minus two, confirming the approximation is accurate to a couple percent.
tbl3_2: A three-row table comparing the exact value, the collocation approximation, and the Galerkin approximation of the solution at the central point x equal zero, with absolute errors; both two-coefficient methods reproduce the maximum value near 0.183, with Galerkin slightly more accurate (error about three ten-thousandths versus six ten-thousandths for collocation).
fig3_2: Two side-by-side line plots over the interval from minus one to one for the reaction-diffusion problem. Left panel: the exact solution, an inverted-bell curve peaking near 0.18 at the center and vanishing at both endpoints, overlaid with the collocation and Galerkin approximations, all three essentially coinciding; the collocation points at x equal zero and x equal one half are marked. Right panel: the error profiles of both methods, where the Galerkin error stays uniformly closer to zero across the whole interval than the collocation error, illustrating Galerkin's better global accuracy.
fig3_3: Side-by-side schematic comparing the support of finite element and spectral basis functions. The left panel shows a finite element hat function: a piecewise-linear triangular spike that is nonzero only over two adjacent mesh elements (marked along a tick-spaced axis) and zero everywhere else, labeled local support. The right panel shows a spectral basis function: a high-frequency polynomial that oscillates up and down across the entire domain, labeled global support. The contrast conveys that finite element bases act locally while spectral bases influence the solution everywhere.
fig3_4: A three-column schematic illustrating refinement strategies, each showing a before state above and an after state below joined by a downward arrow. Left, h-refinement: a coarse two-cell mesh becomes a finer four-cell mesh of equal-width elements, labeled smaller elements. Middle, r-refinement: a uniform four-cell mesh becomes one with the same number of cells redistributed so points cluster on the sides, labeled adaptive redistribution. Right, p-refinement: a low-degree curve labeled p equals two becomes a high-degree oscillating curve labeled p equals eight on the same single element, labeled higher polynomial degree, which is the strategy spectral methods use.
